message.content:
**“Clean gold” is usually called **99.9% pure** because that is the practical standard most markets use for **fine gold**—often marked **999** or **24K**—rather than true 100% purity.[2][3][4]**

Gold is hard to refine to absolute perfection outside a laboratory, and even very high-purity gold typically contains trace impurities.[2][5] In practice, the **millesimal fineness** system measures purity in parts per thousand, so **999 = 99.9%** and **9999 = 99.99%**.[2][4] Most commercial “pure” gold is therefore treated as **99.9% pure**, while some bullion products are made to **99.99%**.[2][3][5]

The reason it stops at 99.9% is partly **technical** and partly **conventional**: refining to near-total purity is difficult and expensive, and the precious-metals industry has adopted **999** as the standard cutoff for fine gold.[2][4][5] Pure gold is also very soft, so for jewelry it is often alloyed with other metals for durability, which is why jewelry is commonly less than 24K.[3][6]
